[JISHUMI:v10p7280/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الحسن وجماعة | reports | They say it was revealed when Ibn Umm Maktūm interrupted the Prophet's effort to convert Meccan leaders; the Prophet turned back to them and God rebuked him.

[JISHUMI:v10p7281/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The blind man might purify himself through good deeds and avoiding sins, or remember God’s signs and benefit from that remembrance.

[TABRISI:80:1-23#2/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | God shows great courtesy: He does not directly say “you frowned,” but shifts to direct address only after passing over the frown.
[TABRISI:80:20/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · المرتضى علم الهدى | rejects | Al-Murtada rejects identifying the passage's subject as the Prophet: the text does not name him, and frowning at a believing seeker or preferring rich people to the poor conflicts with his noble character.
[TABRISI:80:20/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · قيل | reports | The passage is said to have been revealed about Ibn Umm Maktum, also named Abdullah ibn Shurayh ibn Malik ibn Rabiʿa al-Fihri, when he came as the Prophet was urging Quraysh leaders toward Islam.
[TABRISI:80:20/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · قيل | reports | The Prophet was speaking with ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa, Abu Jahl, al-ʿAbbas, Ubayy, and Umayya ibn Khalaf when Ibn Umm Maktum repeatedly asked to be taught; the Prophet turned away, thinking the leaders might scorn a following of blind people and slaves.
[TABRISI:80:20/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Afterward the Prophet honored Ibn Umm Maktum, greeted him as the man for whom his Lord had reproached him, asked about his needs, and appointed him deputy in Medina twice.

[QURTUBI-FULL:80:1-4#2/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | On the primary reading, “he” is Ibn Umm Maktum, who may be purified by the Qur'an and religious instruction, gaining purity and losing ignorance.
[QURTUBI-FULL:80:1-4#2/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Alternatively, “he” refers to the unbeliever: the Prophet hoped he might accept Islam, but could not know whether that hope would come true.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:80:3-8/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The question means, how could you know his state? He may purify himself from sins by what he learns from you; this hints that the Prophet turned away to help another become purified.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:80:3-8/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · قيل | reports | Another view makes the pronoun refer to the unbeliever: the Prophet hoped to purify and admonish him by conversion, and so turned from the other man, though success was uncertain.

[NASAFI-FULL:v4p317/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The blind man might purify himself by hearing the Prophet and shedding the stain of ignorance.

[SAMIN-DURR:80:3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The apparent analysis treats laʿalla like an interrogative because both convey a request and permit suspension: the sense is that he does not know whether purification or remembrance is hoped for.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p319#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The blind man might attain inner purification, or be admonished and deterred from forbidden acts so that the reminder benefits him.

[BURSEVI:v10p258/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | A pause is appropriate after this question: what follows is a new statement, not its object.

[BURSEVI:v10p258/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Even if the Prophet sought a greater benefit, his action outwardly suggested preferring the rich and disregarding the poor man’s hurt, so God reproached him for leaving the better course.

[BURSEVI:v10p258/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Although God knows the outcome, laʿalla in speech of the mighty can express certainty; alternatively it conveys hope from the Prophet’s perspective to stress that neglecting a hoped-for seeker is impermissible.

[ALUSI-FULL:v30p39#3/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Purification here is his cleansing himself of some traces of sin through the religious teachings he learns.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p39#3/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Calling Ibn Umm Maktum the blind man highlights his excuse for interrupting the Prophet's speech while he was occupied with the people, and invites compassion toward him.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p39#3/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another explanation sees the initial third-person wording followed by direct address as heightened censure, like publicly complaining and then confronting the offender with blame and proof.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p39#3/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The description also hints that every weak person deserves the consideration shown to someone in his condition, rather than restricting the lesson to this particular blind man.

[ALUSI-FULL:v30p39#3/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الحسن وأبو عمران الجوني وعيسى وبعض القراء | reports | Al-Hasan, Abu Imran al-Jawni, and Isa read with one hamza, while some readers use two articulated hamzas; in both readings the hamza is an interrogative of repudiation.

[ALUSI-FULL:v30p40/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | A further view says the alluded person was already purified from sins and receptive to admonition.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p40/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | rejects | Some make the pronoun refer to the disbeliever, with hope attributed to the Prophet, who hoped for his conversion and so turned from the blind man; al-Alusi rejects this because the disbeliever was not previously mentioned and the pronoun is singular despite the group addressed, though a report says the person was one.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p105/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The clause “what makes you know?” is circumstantial in relation to the preceding passage.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p105/r10] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Ibn ʿĀshūr quotes the Prophet saying that if his companions remained as they were with him after leaving, angels would shake their hands; he uses it as an example of guidance increasing believers’ spiritual rank.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p105/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The formula combines interrogative mā with causative darā; it means “what makes you know?” and is like “what made you know?” in 69:3 or “what makes you perceive?” in 6:109. | mentions 69:3, 6:109

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p105/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib says that whenever the Quran uses “what made you know,” it gives an explanation afterward.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p105/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The explanation may be explicit, as here and in 97:2–3, or the following wording may instead convey awe, as in 101:10 and 69:3. | mentions 97:2, 97:3, 101:10, 69:3
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p105/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · أبو علي الفارسي | reports | Abu Ali al-Farisi holds that laʿalla suspends the governance of verbs of the heart because hope, like interrogation, expresses a request.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p105/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | With its object governance suspended, يدريك no longer takes three objects; the causative form leaves it with one, and the following clause is independent.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p105/r9] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The man may gain further purification if guided: faith can deepen and lead to good deeds, adding the law’s virtues and noble character beyond initial belief.
